solution:
The correct matching is:

| Column 1 | Column 2 | Column 3 |
|---|---|---|
| Farsightedness | Far away object can be seen clearly | Convex lens |
| Presbyopia | Problem of old age | Bifocal lens |
| Nearsightedness | Nearby object can be seen clearly | Concave lens |

**Nearsightedness (myopia).** The chapter states that in this defect "the eye can see nearby objects clearly but the distant objects appear indistinct", so the far point of the eye is no longer at infinity but shifts closer to the eye, and the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina. "This defect can be corrected by using spectacles with concave lens of proper focal length." The concave lens diverges the incident rays first, and the eye lens can then converge these diverged rays on to the retina. The focal length of a concave lens is negative, so a lens of negative power is required.

**Farsightedness (hypermetropia).** Here "the human eye can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly", so the near point is no longer at 25 cm but shifts farther away, and images of nearby objects get formed behind the retina. "This defect can be corrected by using a convex lens with proper focal length", which converges the rays before they reach the eye lens. The focal length of a convex lens is positive, so these spectacles have positive power.

**Presbyopia.** The chapter says "Generally, the focusing power of the eye lens decreases with age. The muscles near the lens lose their ability to change the focal length of the lens. The near point of the lens shifts farther from the eye. Because of this old people cannot see nearby objects clearly." It is therefore the problem of old age, and the bifocal lens is the remaining entry of Column 3.

[Note: the chapter introduces the bifocal lens for people who suffer from nearsightedness AND farsightedness together — "In such lenses, the upper part is concave lens and corrects nearsightedness while the lower part is a convex lens which corrects the farsightedness." It does not state in so many words that presbyopia is corrected by a bifocal lens. In this table the bifocal lens is the only Column 3 entry left once the concave lens is matched to nearsightedness and the convex lens to farsightedness.]

The figure to be drawn is a double convex lens with both its surfaces shown as parts of two spheres, and the following marked on it: the two centres of curvature \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), the two radii of curvature \(R_1\) and \(R_2\), the principal axis drawn as the straight line through \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), the optical centre \(O\) where that line cuts the lens, the two principal foci \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) marked on the principal axis on either side of the lens, and the focal length \(f\) marked as the distance from \(O\) to \(F\). This is figure 7.3 together with figures 7.4 and 7.5 of the chapter.

The terms, as the chapter defines them:

**Centre of curvature (C)** — "The centres of spheres whose parts form surfaces of the lenses are called centres of curvatures of the lenses." A lens with both surfaces spherical has two centres of curvature, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\).

**Radius of curvature (R)** — "The radii (\(R_1\) and \(R_2\)) of the spheres whose parts form surfaces of the lenses are called the radii of curvature of the lens."

**Principal axis** — "The imaginary line passing through both centres of curvature is called the principal axis of the lens."

**Optical centre (O)** — "The point inside a lens on the principal axis, through which light rays pass without changing their path is called the optical centre of a lens."

**Principal focus (F)** — for a convex lens, light rays parallel to the principal axis "converge to a point on the principal axis" after refraction, and that point is the principal focus; for a concave lens the refracted rays diverge "in such a way that they appear to be coming out of a point on the principal axis", and that point is its principal focus. A lens has two principal foci, \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), one on each side.

**Focal length (f)** — "The distance between the optical centre and principal focus of a lens is called its focal length."

The object must be kept **at \(2F_1\)**, that is, at a distance equal to twice the focal length of the convex lens, measured from the optical centre on the object side.

The chapter's table of images formed by convex lenses gives this directly: when the position of the object is "At \(2F_1\)", the position of the image is "At \(2F_2\)", the size of the image is "Same size" and the nature of the image is "Real and inverted".

This also follows from the chapter's own lens formula. Putting \(u = -2f\) in \(\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}\) gives \(\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{-2f} = \frac{2 - 1}{2f} = \frac{1}{2f}\), so \(v = 2f\). The image distance is positive, so the image is formed on the other side of the lens at \(2F_2\) and is real. The magnification is \(M = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{2f}{-2f} = -1\), so the image is of the same size as the object and, the sign being negative, it is inverted.

**The figure to be drawn:** draw the principal axis and the convex lens with \(O\) at its centre, and mark \(F_1\), \(2F_1\) on the left and \(F_2\), \(2F_2\) on the right. Stand the object \(AB\) upright on the axis exactly at \(2F_1\). Draw two rays from the top point \(B\): one parallel to the principal axis, which after refraction passes through \(F_2\), and one through the optical centre \(O\), which goes on without changing its direction. These two refracted rays meet at \(B'\) at \(2F_2\), below the axis. Drop a perpendicular from \(B'\) to the axis to get \(A'\). The inverted image \(A'B'\) is then of exactly the same length as \(AB\).

A simple microscope is "a convex lens with small focal length" which "produces a virtual, erect and bigger image of an object", and the chapter notes that "one can get a 20 times larger image of an object using such microscopes."

The parts a watch repairer has to work on are extremely small. The chapter explains that "the apparent size of an object depends on the angle subtended by the object at the eye", and that the nearest an object can be brought to a normal eye and still be seen clearly is the near point at 25 cm. Held at 25 cm, a watch part subtends so small an angle that its details cannot be made out, and bringing it any closer only makes it blurred.

The simple microscope solves exactly this: the tiny part is placed close to the convex lens, well inside its focal length, and the lens forms a virtual, erect and much enlarged image which the eye can then view comfortably. Because the image is enlarged and erect, the repairer can see the small parts distinctly and can work on them in their true orientation. This is why the chapter lists watch repair as a use of the simple microscope, together with "testing precious gems and finding their defects".

The chapter explains that "the retina in our eyes is made up of many light sensitive cells" and that "these cells are shaped like a rod and like a cone."

The two kinds of cell do different jobs. "The rod like cells respond to the intensity of light and give information about the brightness or dimness of the object to the brain. The conical cells respond to the colour and give information about the colour of the object to the brain." So colour is sensed by the conical cells alone.

The reason follows from how sensitive each kind is: "Rod like cells respond to faint light also but conical cells do not." In dim light only the rod cells are excited, and since the rods report brightness and not colour, the brain receives information only about how bright or dim the object is. Only when the light is bright enough do the conical cells get excited and send colour information to the brain. "Thus we perceive colours only in bright light."

The chapter defines the near point: "The minimum distance of an object from a normal eye, at which it is clearly visible without stress on the eye, is called as minimum distance of distinct vision. The position of the object at this distance is called the near point of the eye, for a normal human eye, the near point is at 25 cm."

To see a nearby object clearly, the eye lens has to become more rounded so that its focal length decreases and the image is still formed on the retina — the chapter calls this ability "the power of accommodation": "the capacity of the lens to change its focal length as per need."

The limit is stated by the chapter itself: "Although the elastic lens can change its focal length, to increase or decrease it, it can not do so beyond a limit." The distance between the lens and the retina is fixed, so as an object is brought nearer the lens must keep shortening its focal length. At 25 cm the lens is already at the limit of that adjustment. If the object is brought closer than 25 cm, the lens cannot become any more rounded, its focal length cannot be shortened enough, and the image is no longer formed on the retina. The object therefore appears blurred and the eye is strained, even though the object subtends a bigger angle at the eye at that closer distance.

A telescope "is used to see distant objects clearly in their magnified form", and the chapter says "the telescopes used to observe astronomical sources like the stars and the planets are called astronomical telescopes." Of the two types it lists — the refracting telescope, which "uses lenses", and the reflecting telescope, which "uses mirrors and also lenses" — the one that works by refraction of light is the **refracting telescope** (figure 7.18).

**Construction.** It is made of two convex lenses, the objective and the eyepiece. The objective lens "has large diameter and larger focal length". The eyepiece is the smaller of the two: "the size of the eyepiece is smaller and its focal length is also less." "Both the lenses are fitted inside a metallic tube in such a way that the distance between them can be changed", and "the principal axes of both the lenses are along the same straight line."

**Working.** Light coming from a distant astronomical object falls on the objective. Because the objective has a large diameter, "maximum amount of light coming from the distant object can be collected". The rays are refracted by the objective, which forms an image of the distant object inside the tube. That image then serves as the object for the second lens: "the image formed by the objective acts as object for the eye piece which forms the final image." The eyepiece, being a convex lens of short focal length, refracts the light a second time and forms the final magnified image that the observer sees. The magnification can be adjusted by sliding the lenses to change the separation between them, and "generally, using the same objective but different eye pieces, different magnification can be obtained."

[Note: the chapter does not give a formula for the magnification of a telescope, and it does not state whether the final image is erect or inverted, so those are not asserted here.]

| Point of difference | Nearsightedness (Myopia) | Farsightedness (Hypermetropia) |
|---|---|---|
| What is seen clearly | "The eye can see nearby objects clearly but the distant objects appear indistinct." | "The human eye can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly." |
| Which point has shifted | "The far point of the eye is not at infinity but shifts closer to the eye." | "The near point of the eye is no longer at 25 cm but shifts farther away." |
| Where the image is formed | The image of a distant object forms in front of the retina. | The images of nearby objects get formed behind the retina. |
| First cause | "The curvature of the cornea and the eye lens increases", so the converging power of the lens remains large. | "Curvature of the cornea and the eye lens decreases so that, the converging power of the lens becomes less." |
| Second cause | "The eyeball elongates so that the distance between the lens and the retina increases." | "Due to the flattening of the eye ball the distance between the lens and retina decreases." |
| Corrected by | A concave lens of proper focal length, which diverges the incident rays. | A convex lens of proper focal length, which converges the incident rays. |
| Power of the corrective lens | Negative, since the focal length of a concave lens is negative. | Positive, since the focal length of a convex lens is positive. |

| Point of difference | Convex (double convex) lens | Concave (double concave) lens |
|---|---|---|
| Surfaces | "Two spherical surfaces which are puffed up outwards." | "Both surfaces spherical on the inside." |
| Thickness | "Thicker near the centre as compared to the edges." | "Thinner at the centre as compared to its edges." |
| Effect on parallel rays | Rays parallel to the principal axis "converge to a point on the principal axis" after refraction. | Rays parallel to the principal axis "diverge after refraction in such a way that they appear to be coming out of a point on the principal axis." |
| Name for that behaviour | Converging lens. | Divergent lens. |
| Sign of the focal length | Positive. | Negative. |
| Nature of the image | Real and inverted for every object position from infinity down to \(F_1\); virtual and erect only when the object lies between \(F_1\) and \(O\). | "The image formed by a concave lens is always virtual, erect and smaller than the object." |
| Use in spectacles | Used to correct farsightedness. | Used to correct nearsightedness. |

**Function of the iris.** The chapter describes the iris as "a dark, fleshy screen" behind the cornea, and says "there is a small hole of changing diameter at the centre of the Iris which is called the pupil." The function follows: "The pupil controls the amount of light entering the eye. If the light falling on the eye is too bright, pupil contracts while if the light is dim, it widens." So the iris regulates the size of the pupil, and through it the quantity of light that is allowed into the eye — cutting the light down when it is too bright and letting more in when it is dim, so that the retina always receives a workable amount of light.

**Function of the muscles connected to the lens.** These muscles change the shape, and therefore the focal length, of the crystalline lens so that the image always falls on the retina whatever the distance of the object. The chapter describes both settings: "While seeing objects at large, infinite distances, the lens of the eye becomes flat and its focal length increases", and "while seeing nearby objects the lens becomes more rounded and its focal length decreases. This way we can see objects clearly irrespective of their distance." It names this ability: "The capacity of the lens to change its focal length as per need is called its power of accommodation."

That the muscles are what do this is confirmed by what happens when they fail. In nearsightedness "the muscles near the lens can not relax so that the converging power of the lens remains large", and in presbyopia "the muscles near the lens lose their ability to change the focal length of the lens", so that the near point shifts farther from the eye.

**Given:** power of the lens \(P = +1.5\ \text{D}\).
**To find:** the focal length \(f\), the type of the lens, and the defect of vision.

The chapter gives the power of a lens as \(P = \frac{1}{f\ (\text{m})}\), with \(f\) expressed in metres and the unit of power the dioptre. Therefore

\(f = \frac{1}{P} = \frac{1}{1.5} = 0.666\ldots\ \text{m} \approx +0.67\ \text{m}\)

So the focal length is about \(+0.67\ \text{m}\), that is about \(67\ \text{cm}\).

**Type of lens.** The focal length has come out positive, and the chapter's sign convention states that "the focal length of a convex lens is positive while that of a concave lens is negative." The prescribed lens is therefore a **convex (converging) lens**.

**Defect of vision.** The chapter says that farsightedness "can be corrected by using a convex lens with proper focal length" and that "the focal length of a convex lens is positive thus the spectacles used to correct farsightedness has positive power." A prescription of \(+1.5\ \text{D}\) is a positive power, so the defect must be **farsightedness (hypermetropia)**.

The textbook prints the answer to this question as "\(+0.67\) m, farsightedness", and this derivation agrees with it in both parts.

**Given:** height of the object \(h_1 = 5\ \text{cm}\); the object is \(25\ \text{cm}\) from the lens, and since the object is always placed to the left of the lens and distances measured to the left of \(O\) are negative, \(u = -25\ \text{cm}\); the lens is converging, so \(f = +10\ \text{cm}\).
**To find:** the image distance \(v\), the height of the image \(h_2\), and the type of the image.

**Position.** From the lens formula \(\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}\),

\(\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{-25} = \frac{5 - 2}{50} = \frac{3}{50}\)

\(v = \frac{50}{3} = 16.67 \approx 16.7\ \text{cm}\)

**Type.** The image distance is positive, so by the sign convention the image is formed \(16.7\ \text{cm}\) to the right of the lens, that is on the side opposite to the object. The image is therefore **real**, and being real it is inverted.

**Size.** The magnification is \(M = \frac{h_2}{h_1} = \frac{v}{u}\), so

\(M = \frac{50/3}{-25} = -\frac{2}{3}\)

\(h_2 = M \times h_1 = -\frac{2}{3} \times 5 = -\frac{10}{3} = -3.33 \approx -3.3\ \text{cm}\)

The image is \(3.3\ \text{cm}\) tall. The negative sign means it lies below the principal axis, that is the image is inverted, and it is smaller than the \(5\ \text{cm}\) object.

**Answer.** The image is formed \(16.7\ \text{cm}\) from the lens on the far side, is \(3.3\ \text{cm}\) tall, and is real and inverted.

This agrees with the chapter's own table. Here \(2f = 20\ \text{cm}\), so an object at \(25\ \text{cm}\) is "Beyond \(2F_1\)", and the table says the image of such an object lies "Between \(F_2\) and \(2F_2\)" — that is between \(10\ \text{cm}\) and \(20\ \text{cm}\), and \(16.7\ \text{cm}\) does lie between them — with size "Smaller" and nature "Real and inverted".

The textbook prints the answer as "\(16.7\) cm, \(3.3\) cm, Real", and this derivation agrees with it. The book gives the height as a magnitude; the calculation shows the sign is negative, which is what tells us the image is inverted.

**Given:** three lenses of powers \(P_1 = 2\ \text{D}\), \(P_2 = 2.5\ \text{D}\) and \(P_3 = 1.7\ \text{D}\), kept touching one another in a row.
**To find:** the total power \(P\) of the combination.

The chapter states the rule for lenses kept in contact: "If the powers of the two lenses are \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) then the effective power of their combination is \(P = P_1 + P_2\). Thus, when two lenses are kept touching each other, the power of the combined lens is equal to the sum of their individual powers." The same addition is applied here to the three lenses, which are likewise kept touching:

\(P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 = 2 + 2.5 + 1.7 = 6.2\ \text{D}\)

The total power of the lens combination is \(6.2\ \text{D}\).

The power is positive, so the combination behaves as a converging lens, and its effective focal length is \(f = \frac{1}{P} = \frac{1}{6.2} \approx 0.16\ \text{m}\), that is about \(16\ \text{cm}\).

The textbook prints the answer as "\(6.2\) D", and this derivation agrees with it.

[Note: the chapter states the addition rule for two lenses in contact. This question applies it to three lenses kept touching in a row, which is the same rule used one more time.]

**Given:** the object is \(60\ \text{cm}\) from the lens. By the sign convention the object is on the left of the lens and distances to the left of \(O\) are negative, so \(u = -60\ \text{cm}\). The image is virtual and lies \(20\ \text{cm}\) in front of the lens, that is on the same side as the object, so it too is to the left of \(O\) and \(v = -20\ \text{cm}\).
**To find:** the focal length \(f\), and whether the lens is converging or diverging.

From the lens formula \(\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}\),

\(\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{-20} - \frac{1}{-60} = -\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{60} = \frac{-3 + 1}{60} = -\frac{2}{60} = -\frac{1}{30}\)

\(f = -30\ \text{cm}\)

**Type of lens.** The focal length is negative, and the chapter's sign convention states that "the focal length of a convex lens is positive while that of a concave lens is negative." The lens is therefore a **concave lens**, and the chapter calls such a lens a divergent lens because rays parallel to its principal axis "go away from one another (diverge) after refraction." So it is a **diverging lens**.

**Cross-check.** The magnification is \(M = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{-20}{-60} = +\frac{1}{3}\). The sign is positive and the value is less than one, so the image is erect and smaller than the object — exactly what the chapter says of this lens: "The image formed by a concave lens is always virtual, erect and smaller than the object." The image also lies between the optical centre and the focus, at \(20\ \text{cm}\) with the focus at \(30\ \text{cm}\), as the chapter's table for concave lenses requires.

The textbook prints the answer as "\(-30\) cm, lens is diverging or concave", and this derivation agrees with it.
